lead: A modulator must make new frequencies, f<sub>c</sub> + f<sub>m</sub> and f<sub>c</sub> − f<sub>m</sub>, that are in neither input. A linear circuit cannot do this; a nonlinear one can. A diode or transistor run on the curved part of its characteristic has a current with a term in the square of its input voltage, and that square contains the product of carrier and message. A square-law modulator uses one such device and a band-pass filter to make AM with carrier. A balanced modulator uses two devices in push-pull so that the carrier cancels, giving DSB-SC.
prereq: You need: the AM and DSB-SC spectra from AM: modulation index, spectrum and power and DSB-SC modulation and coherent detection.

blocks.text: Near its bias point the current i of a nonlinear device can be written as a power series in its input voltage v. For a small input the cube and higher terms are negligible:
i in mA, v in volts; a<sub>0</sub> is the bias current (mA), a<sub>1</sub> the slope (mA/V) and a<sub>2</sub> the square-law coefficient (mA/V²).

Apply v = A<sub>c</sub> cos ω<sub>c</sub>t + A<sub>m</sub> cos ω<sub>m</sub>t, where ω = 2πf. The linear term a<sub>1</sub>v only copies the inputs. The square term gives, with cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2 and 2 cos A cos B = cos(A − B) + cos(A + B):

items: The cross product 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub> cos ω<sub>c</sub>t cos ω<sub>m</sub>t = a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub>[cos(ω<sub>c</sub> − ω<sub>m</sub>)t + cos(ω<sub>c</sub> + ω<sub>m</sub>)t]: the two sidebands.

blocks.text: Only the cross product makes sidebands. The figure plots every output line of the worked example on one frequency axis.

Carrier and message are added and applied to the device. A band-pass filter (a tuned LC tank) centred on f<sub>c</sub> with bandwidth 2W keeps the carrier a<sub>1</sub>A<sub>c</sub> cos ω<sub>c</sub>t, which comes from the linear term, and the two sidebands of a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub> each, which come from the square term. Comparing with A<sub>c</sub>'[1 + m cos ω<sub>m</sub>t] cos ω<sub>c</sub>t, whose sidebands are mA<sub>c</sub>'/2:
m is the modulation index. It contains no A<sub>c</sub>: a bigger carrier raises the output, not the modulation depth.

The filter must reject DC, the message at f<sub>m</sub> and its harmonic at 2f<sub>m</sub>, and the harmonic at 2f<sub>c</sub>. The lowest wanted frequency is f<sub>c</sub> − W and the highest unwanted one below it is 2W, so f<sub>c</sub> − W > 2W, that is f<sub>c</sub> > 3W. Above, 2f<sub>c</sub> is far from f<sub>c</sub> + W. For a large message the a<sub>3</sub>v³ term adds lines at f<sub>c</sub> ± 2f<sub>m</sub>, so these modulators run at small m.

sections.h3: The balanced modulator and the diode ring

blocks.text: Two matched square-law devices receive the same carrier but opposite message: v<sub>1</sub> = c(t) + m(t) and v<sub>2</sub> = c(t) − m(t), with c(t) = A<sub>c</sub> cos ω<sub>c</sub>t. A centre-tapped output transformer takes the difference of their currents:

a<sub>1</sub>c(t) appears equally in i<sub>1</sub> and i<sub>2</sub>, so the subtraction removes it; so do a<sub>0</sub>, a<sub>2</sub>c² and a<sub>2</sub>m². What is left is the message and the product term.

With a tone, 4a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub> cos ω<sub>c</sub>t cos ω<sub>m</sub>t = 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub>[cos(ω<sub>c</sub> − ω<sub>m</sub>)t + cos(ω<sub>c</sub> + ω<sub>m</sub>)t]. A band-pass filter at f<sub>c</sub> removes the message term 2a<sub>1</sub>m(t), and the output is DSB-SC. If the devices are not matched, part of the carrier survives (carrier leakage), so practical balanced modulators have a balance control.

The ring modulator uses four diodes in a ring with centre-tapped transformers. A large carrier switches the diodes so that the message is multiplied by a square wave p(t) that flips between +1 and −1 at fc. Since p(t) = (4/π)[cos ωct − (1/3) cos 3ωct + …], the output holds DSB-SC at fc with amplitude (2/π)Am per sideband and weaker copies around 3fc, 5fc, which a band-pass filter removes. The ring is passive and works into the hundreds of megahertz; sold as a double-balanced mixer it is also the mixer of most receivers.

examples.question: A device has i = 10v + 2v² mA (v in volts). Its input is v = 2 cos(2π × 100 × 10³t) + 0.5 cos(2π × 10³t) V. Find every output line, the carrier and sideband currents after a band-pass filter at 100 kHz, and m.
steps: a<sub>1</sub> = 10 mA/V, a<sub>2</sub> = 2 mA/V², A<sub>c</sub> = 2 V at 100 kHz, A<sub>m</sub> = 0.5 V at 1 kHz.
Linear term: 10 × 2 = 20 mA at 100 kHz and 10 × 0.5 = 5 mA at 1 kHz.
Harmonics: 2 × 2²/2 = 4 mA at 200 kHz and 2 × 0.5²/2 = 0.25 mA at 2 kHz.
Sidebands: a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub> = 2 × 2 × 0.5 = 2 mA each, at 99 kHz and 101 kHz.
After the filter (99 to 101 kHz): carrier 20 mA, sidebands 2 mA each.
m = 2 × 2/20 = 0.2; check 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>m</sub>/a<sub>1</sub> = 2 × 2 × 0.5/10 = 0.2. Through a 1 kΩ tank this is 20 V of carrier with 2 V sidebands.
f<sub>c</sub> > 3W: 100 kHz > 3 kHz, so the 2 kHz line is far below the 99 kHz edge.
examples.answer: Lines: 4.25 mA DC, 5 mA at 1 kHz, 0.25 mA at 2 kHz, 2 mA at 99 and 101 kHz, 20 mA at 100 kHz, 4 mA at 200 kHz. Output: 20 mA carrier, 2 mA sidebands, m = 0.2.

examples.question: The same devices form a balanced modulator with v<sub>1</sub>,2 = 2 cos ω<sub>c</sub>t ± 0.5 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t. Find the output lines. If one device has a<sub>1</sub> = 10.5 mA/V instead of 10, how much carrier leaks, and how far below each sideband is it?
steps: Message term 2a<sub>1</sub>A<sub>m</sub> = 2 × 10 × 0.5 = 10 mA at 1 kHz (removed by the band-pass filter).
Sidebands 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub> = 2 × 2 × 2 × 0.5 = 4 mA each at 99 and 101 kHz, twice the single-device value.
Carrier: a<sub>1</sub>A<sub>c</sub> in each current; with a<sub>1</sub> = 10.5 and 10 the difference is (10.5 − 10) × 2 = 1 mA at 100 kHz.
Ratio: 20 log(4/1) = 12.0 dB below each sideband.
examples.answer: DSB-SC with 4 mA sidebands at 99 and 101 kHz; a 5 % mismatch leaks a 1 mA carrier, only 12 dB below the sidebands.

traps: The AM output carrier comes from the linear term a<sub>1</sub>v, not from squaring; the square term alone gives sidebands, DC and harmonics.
m = 2a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>m</sub>/a<sub>1</sub> has no A<sub>c</sub> in it. Doubling the carrier does not change m.
The balanced modulator removes the carrier, not the message term 2a<sub>1</sub>m(t); the output band-pass filter removes that.

quiz.q: Write the square-law model of a device and the unit of each coefficient.
quiz.a: i = a<sub>0</sub> + a<sub>1</sub>v + a<sub>2</sub>v², with a<sub>0</sub> in mA, a<sub>1</sub> in mA/V and a<sub>2</sub> in mA/V² (or the same in amperes).

quiz.q: A device has i = 2v + 0.1v² mA and v = 3 cos ω<sub>c</sub>t + 0.4 cos ω<sub>m</sub>t V. Find the carrier, sideband and m.
quiz.a: Carrier a<sub>1</sub>A<sub>c</sub> = 6 mA; each sideband a<sub>2</sub>A<sub>c</sub>A<sub>m</sub> = 0.1 × 3 × 0.4 = 0.12 mA; m = 2 × 0.12/6 = 0.04.

quiz.q: In the balanced modulator, why does the carrier cancel while the sidebands add?
quiz.a: Both devices see +c(t), so a<sub>1</sub>c(t) and a<sub>2</sub>c² are equal in i<sub>1</sub> and i<sub>2</sub> and vanish in i<sub>1</sub> − i<sub>2</sub>. The cross term 2a<sub>2</sub>c(t)m(t) has the sign of m, which is opposite in the two devices, so it doubles.

quiz.q: A ring modulator multiplies a 1 V tone by a ±1 square wave at 100 kHz. Find the sideband amplitudes at f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub> and 3f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub>.
quiz.a: p(t) = (4/π)[cos ω<sub>c</sub>t − (1/3) cos 3ω<sub>c</sub>t + …]. At f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub> each line is 2/π = 0.637 V; at 3f<sub>c</sub> ± f<sub>m</sub> each is 2/(3π) = 0.212 V.

quiz.q: Why do practical balanced modulators include a balance control?
quiz.a: Real devices never match exactly. The example's 5 % slope mismatch leaks a carrier only 12 dB below the sidebands; trimming the balance cancels the leak.

beyond: The Gilbert cell inside multiplier and mixer chips is a balanced modulator built from differential pairs. Modern transmitters reach RF through an I/Q modulator, two balanced mixers in quadrature. Search next for Gilbert cell and double-balanced mixer.
